opus-5.5.text:
I think Jin Yong's novels shaped me in ways I only really understood later in life. I read them as a kid, mostly for the excitement: the martial arts, the adventures, the rivalries. Looking back, though, a few ideas really stayed with me.

The first is the idea of practicing your craft. In Jin Yong's world, nobody becomes great overnight. Even when a character stumbles onto a secret manual or meets a great master, they still have to train for years and internalize the skill until it becomes part of them. Research feels very similar to me. You read papers, you run experiments, most of them fail, and slowly you build intuition. There's no shortcut. You keep practicing until one day you can see the problem more clearly than before.

The second is the idea that the highest level of skill is formless. Think of Feng Qingyang teaching Linghu Chong the Dugu Nine Swords: the point isn't to memorize moves but to understand the principle so well that you can respond to anything. In AI that matters a lot, because the field changes so quickly. The specific technique you mastered five years ago may be obsolete today. What lasts is the underlying understanding: how to frame a problem, how to think about data, how to tell what really matters.

The third is about character. Many of Jin Yong's heroes, like Guo Jing, aren't the smartest people in the room. They succeed because they're sincere, persistent, and they care about something bigger than themselves. "The greatest hero is one who serves the country and the people" is a line I still think about. As a researcher, I hope the work I do eventually helps people and isn't just about publishing another paper or winning a benchmark.

And honestly, there's also the joy of the jianghu, a world full of interesting people with different styles and schools. The research community feels a bit like that. Different labs have different "martial arts schools," you exchange ideas, you compete, and sometimes you become friends with your rivals. That makes the journey a lot more fun.

r001.rationale: He describes being drawn in as a child by the novels’ adventures and martial arts, and later likens their jianghu to an engaging world of varied people and styles.

r002.rationale: He discusses martial arts as part of the novels but does not say they prompted him to study Chinese martial arts.

fable-5.1.text:
Jin Yong gave me a lot, really more than I understood at the time. I read all of his novels when I was a kid in Taiwan, and I think the first thing they taught me was about the long road of becoming good at something. Those characters are never born masters. Guo Jing is the slow one, the one everybody thinks is a bit dumb, and he just keeps practicing, keeps showing up, and in the end he becomes the greatest. That stayed with me. When I was a student and later doing research, I was never the fastest person in the room, so I always felt I had to be Guo Jing. Just keep going, keep training, and trust that the accumulation matters.

The second thing is the way his heroes carry responsibility. Guo Jing defending Xiangyang, Qiao Feng caught between two peoples, the idea that a true xia acts for the country and for the people, not for himself. That sounds very old-fashioned, but it shaped how I think about building things. When we do research or build technology, I want it to be useful for a lot of people, not just a clever trick that gets a paper accepted.

And honestly, there is a third thing, which is imagination. Jin Yong built entire worlds with their own rules, their own physics of martial arts, and they feel completely consistent. That is very close to what we are trying to do with simulation and world models today. You are building a world, you decide the rules, and then everything has to be coherent inside it. I think reading those novels as a child made me comfortable with the idea that a constructed world can feel real, and that is something I still carry into my work every day.

r001.rationale: He says Jin Yong’s novels gave him imagination, built coherent worlds, and made him comfortable with the idea that a constructed world can feel real.

r002.rationale: He discusses martial arts as part of the novels’ imagined worlds, but does not say the novels prompted him to study Chinese martial arts.

astra-6.text: I think Jin Yong’s novels influenced the way I think about what it means to be a hero. His characters often face choices where loyalty, friendship, and their own sense of right and wrong pull them in different directions. Being powerful doesn’t necessarily tell you what you should do. That’s what I find compelling: beyond the martial arts and adventure, there’s this question of what kind of person you want to become, and what you’re willing to stand up for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses heroism, moral choices, martial arts, and adventure, but does not say the novels influenced Liu by letting him experience imaginative artistic worlds.

r002.rationale: The response mentions martial arts as part of the novels, but does not state that they prompted Liu to study Chinese martial arts.

sol-6.1.text: I think Jin Yong’s novels influenced my imagination more than anything else. You enter these worlds with their own rules, and you get to know characters through the choices they make—who they trust, what they’re willing to sacrifice, and how they respond when their values come into conflict. The martial arts are exciting, of course, but it’s those human dilemmas that stay with me. They encouraged me to imagine possibilities beyond everyday experience.

r001.rationale: He says the novels influenced his imagination and describes entering their imaginative worlds.

r002.rationale: He mentions martial arts as exciting, but does not say the novels prompted him to study Chinese martial arts.
